strengths: The problem — accelerating next-token-prediction AR image generation via speculative decoding — is important and relatively underexplored; the proposed combination of multi-resolution drafting (low-res drafter + learned up-sampler + high-res verifier) with spatially-local rejection/expansion is a sensible and novel design in this space (first SD method to exploit a multi-scale prior).

The paper is unusually transparent and honest: it reports that ZipAR (a non-SD baseline) dominates its method in both speed and quality, that EAGLE-2 yields negative speedup on image data, and that LANTERN underperforms relative to its LlamaGen results, with a reasoned explanation (Tar is a stronger/harder-to-approximate model, supported by drafter top-1 accuracy analysis in the supplementary).

Extensive and well-designed ablations: up/down-sampler loss formulations (cross-entropy vs. MSE/LPIPS vs. discriminators), probability pooling, raster-scan vs. local rejection vs. local rejection with expansion, and neighborhood radius l (Fig. 9), plus a latency breakdown (Fig. 7) that clarifies where time is spent and why the 4× setting is most favorable.

Method and implementation details are sufficiently complete for reproducibility: full algorithm (Alg. 1), training recipes, hyperparameters (τ, k, δ, l), and the comparison protocol for sweeping the acceptance threshold are documented; the schematic comparison to SD/LANTERN (Fig. 6) aids understanding.

The framing of local verification (Eq. 6–7) is well-motivated by the observed spatial locality of visual AR models and empirically shown to be necessary (naive local resampling without expansion performs worse).
weaknesses: The headline gains are modest and fragile: 1.22× (512p) and 1.68× (1024p) vs. LANTERN's 1.08×/1.42×, while a training-free baseline (ZipAR) achieves 1.88×/3.65× with near-identical quality. The claimed orthogonality of ZipAR is plausible, but the combined system is never evaluated, leaving the practical value of the added complexity (trained up/down-samplers, extra drafter) in question.

The reported speedups exclude the ~17s MLLM conditioning latency, which is comparable to the entire 512p AR-DTok decoding time (18s). The effective end-to-end speedup at 512p is therefore substantially below 1.22×, which weakens the practical significance of the reported numbers and should be foregrounded rather than relegated to the supplementary.

The acceptance rule (Eq. 5, threshold τ with τ = 1e−4) is a heuristic relaxation with no distributional guarantee; unlike LANTERN's TVD-bounded criterion, MuLo-SD offers no bound on deviation from the target distribution, and FID actually degrades (+0.7 at 512p, +0.4 at 1024p). The claim of 'without compromising quality' is only partially supported.

The comparison protocol is tuned to the method's advantage: the τ operating point is selected post hoc to match LANTERN's GenEval score, which complicates interpreting the speed/quality comparison and introduces selection bias against the baselines.

Evaluation breadth is narrow: a single model family (Tar-1.5B / AR-DTok), one dataset (MS-COCO 5k), and no experiment on LlamaGen, which would enable direct comparison with LANTERN's originally reported results. Generalization beyond Tar (and beyond architectures that ship resolution-specific checkpoints, on which the multi-scale drafting depends) is untested.
Potential domain mismatch: up/down-samplers and LANTERN drafters are trained on LAION-COCO-Aesthetic while evaluation is on MS-COCO; the sensitivity to this choice is not analyzed.

Some baselines may be under-tuned (LANTERN drafter top-1 accuracy of 0.12 at 512p); although the authors provide a justification, the low drafter quality inflates MuLo-SD's relative advantage, and the paper lacks a controlled sensitivity analysis of baseline performance to drafter quality.

Presentation issues: several typos ('rater-scan', 'Validaiton', 'howevere', 'inject the coarse-to-fine'), Eq. 1–2 attribution to [58] vs. the standard Leviathan et al. formulation, and Table 1 mixes FID improvements/degradations ambiguously (LANTERN improves FID while MuLo-SD worsens it, which the text does not squarely acknowledge).

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine problem: existing speculative decoding for AR image generation (LANTERN) ignores the multi-scale and spatial structure of images, and the proposed coarse-to-fine drafting plus local verification is a sensible and reasonably novel combination.

The method section is generally well explained (Fig. 2, Algorithm 1), and the supplementary material is unusually transparent: it reports the drafter Top-1/Top-3 accuracy achieved when porting LANTERN, gives training details for the up/down-samplers, and discusses why LANTERN underperforms on Tar.

The ablations (loss design for up/down-samplers, probability pooling, local rejection vs. raster-scan rejection vs. local expansion with radius l) directly support the design choices, and the latency breakdown in the supplement honestly shows the drafter cost bottleneck at 512p.
Reproducibility appears reasonable: base model, codebases, datasets, hyperparameters (k, delta, tau, l), and training budgets are specified.
weaknesses: The headline contribution is dominated by a much simpler baseline: ZipAR, a training-free parallel decoding method, achieves 3.65x vs. MuLo-SD's 1.68x at 1024p with equal or better GenEval/DPG/FID/HPSv2 (Table 1, Fig. 8). The supplementary explicitly admits 'ZipAR dominates all other methods.' The claim of 'a new state-of-the-art in speculative decoding' holds only within the speculative-decoding subcategory, which weakens the practical significance considerably.

Absolute speedups are modest and inconsistent across resolutions: 1.22x at 512p (vs. 1.08x for LANTERN and 1.88x for ZipAR) and 1.68x at 1024p. The 'up to 1.7x' framing cherry-picks the 1024p setting; the paper's own latency analysis shows the drafter cost makes the 2x setting barely useful.

The method trades away the core guarantee of speculative decoding: with the threshold rule of Eq. (5) (tau swept to a very permissive 1e-4), sampling is no longer distribution-preserving, and quality degrades (FID +0.4/+0.7, HPSv2 -0.7/-1.1 vs. baseline). LANTERN at least bounds TVD; MuLo-SD offers no such bound, and the operating point is selected by matching LANTERN's GenEval, which is a somewhat arbitrary calibration.

The multi-scale component requires training extra up/down-sampler modules (~20-30M parameters each, up to ~24h on 4x A100) plus resolution-specific pipelines, while ZipAR is training-free and needs none of this. The cost/benefit is unfavorable.

Evaluation breadth is limited: all results are on a single base model (Tar-1.5B). No experiments on LlamaGen, where the baselines were originally developed and where acceptance behavior differs; the claimed advantage over LANTERN could be model-specific, and the paper itself shows LANTERN's relative speedup changes drastically between LlamaGen and Tar.

The comparison to LANTERN may be unfair in a subtle way: the LANTERN drafter reaches Top-1 accuracy 0.12-0.22 on Tar (vs. 0.38 on LlamaGen), so baseline performance partly reflects a hard-to-approximate target rather than properties of MuLo-SD; no alternative drafter designs or tuning budgets for the baseline are explored.

Statistical rigor is thin: latency is averaged over 500 prompts with no variance or confidence intervals; FID/HPSv2 on 5k MS-COCO is noisy, and differences of ~0.3-0.7 FID are hard to interpret without error bars.

Minor inconsistencies undermine polish: the main text states delta = 0.4 following the original paper, while the supplement fixes delta = 0.1 'across all experiments'; several typos ('inject the coarse-to-fine approach', 'rater-scan', 'Validaiton').

strengths: Genuinely novel combination for the speculative decoding literature: the paper is, to my knowledge, the first to inject a multi-resolution (coarse-to-fine) drafting prior into next-token speculative decoding for image generation, and to exploit spatial locality for rejection/resampling rather than raster-scan truncation. This is a well-motivated design grounded in the spatial coherence of visual tokens.

The local verification and expansion mechanism (Eqs. 5-7, Fig. 3) is technically sensible and empirically validated: the ablation in Fig. 5c shows that both local rejection and neighborhood expansion are necessary, with raster-scan rejection and naive local rejection clearly worse at matched speedup.

Extensive and transparent experimentation: comparisons against ZipAR, EAGLE-2, and LANTERN at two resolutions, four evaluation metrics (GenEval, DPG-Bench, FID, HPSv2), a Pareto-front sweep over the acceptance threshold (Fig. 8), a latency breakdown (Fig. 7), and ablations over loss design, probability pooling, and expansion radius (Fig. 9).

Honest reporting: the authors openly acknowledge that ZipAR achieves higher speedups, that LANTERN underperforms its original LlamaGen numbers on Tar, and that the 512p setting is bottlenecked by drafter cost. The supplementary provides substantial implementation detail (training recipes, hyperparameters, drafter accuracy measurements) supporting reproducibility.

The contribution is practical and lightweight: up/down-samplers are ~20-30M parameters trained in under 24 hours on 4 A100s, and the method requires no retraining of the target MLLM, integrating cleanly with next-token prediction unified models.
weaknesses: The headline gains are modest and the method is dominated by a simpler, training-free baseline: at 512p MuLo-SD achieves only 1.22x vs ZipAR's 1.88x, and at 1024p 1.68x vs 3.65x, with ZipAR also showing better FID and comparable GenEval. The authors argue orthogonality but never demonstrate the combined system, leaving the practical case for MuLo-SD somewhat weakened.

The method abandons any distributional guarantee: unlike standard speculative decoding (exact) or LANTERN (TVD-bounded relaxation, Eq. 4), the acceptance rule in Eq. 5 is a pure probability-mass threshold with no formal bound on divergence from the target distribution. The paper claims 'comparable' quality but this is only empirically supported at a single tuned operating point.

The operating point selection raises fairness concerns: tau is explicitly swept 'to match LANTERN's GenEval score' (Table 1 caption), i.e., the speedup comparison is made at a quality-matched but post-hoc chosen point, and even then MuLo-SD loses 0.8-1.7 GenEval points and 0.7-1.1 HPSv2 points relative to the exact baseline, with FID worsening by 0.4-0.7.

Evaluation breadth is narrow: all results are on a single model family (Tar-1.5B), which happens to have resolution-specific checkpoints that make multi-scale drafting natural. No results on LlamaGen, VAR-style models, or other AR generators, so generalization of the claims (e.g., 'state-of-the-art in speculative decoding') is unverified.

The paper itself notes the drafter has the same architecture/computational complexity as the target, so speedup derives entirely from the sequence-length quadratic gap; the supplementary latency analysis confirms the drafter is the bottleneck at 512p (overhead ~5%), which limits applicability to settings with small resolution ratios.

Some presentation issues: the claim of 'new state-of-the-art' should be qualified given ZipAR's dominance; terminology alternates between MuLo-SD and MSD (Figs. 5/8/9); the role of delta in the supplementary (0.1) versus main text (0.4 for the LANTERN baseline) is easy to misread; and several passages (e.g., draft model generating 'full rows') require careful reading to parse.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: accelerating next-token-prediction AR image generation in unified MLLMs, where next-scale (VAR-style) approaches do not directly apply. The framing of multi-scale drafting as a way to inject coarse-to-fine structure into speculative decoding is sensible and well-motivated.

The experimental protocol is broad: two models (Tar-1.5B/7B, LlamaGen-XL), two target resolutions (512p, 1024p), and four metrics (GenEval, DPG-Bench, FID, HPSv2), with fair porting of strong baselines (EAGLE-2, LANTERN, ZipAR) and matched-quality operating points obtained by sweeping the acceptance threshold.

Ablations are extensive and cover every major design decision: upsampler loss design (Fig. 5a), probability pooling (5b), raster-scan vs. local vs. expanded-local rejection (5c, Fig. 9), and parallel decoding integration (5d). The supplementary latency breakdown (Fig. 7) is transparent about where time goes and about the fixed drafter cost bottleneck.

The local verification with neighborhood expansion and rejection-island parallel resampling is a clean idea that plausibly exploits spatial locality of visual AR models, and the ablations support both components (teal vs. green vs. pink in Fig. 5c).

The limitations section is honest and substantive (two checkpoints, memory overhead, drafter-verifier distributional alignment), and the supplementary discussion of weaker LANTERN/EAGLE-2 results on Tar includes drafter top-1/3 accuracy analysis rather than hiding the discrepancy.
weaknesses: The method abandons the exactness guarantee of speculative decoding: the threshold criterion in Eq. (5) accepts draft tokens based on pooled probability mass without a residual-distribution correction, so MULO-SD is a lossy acceleration method. There is no theoretical or empirical characterization of the resulting distributional drift (the TVD bound machinery from LANTERN is cited but effectively unused, with k=1000 covering the full codebook), and occasional 'improvements' over the base model (e.g., FID +0.4 at 1024p) are unexplained and likely artifacts.

The headline claim of outperforming parallel decoding is fragile. The training-free ZipAR baseline achieves 3.65x at essentially zero metric degradation at 1024p, versus 3.90x for MULO-SD with small quality drops; on LlamaGen, MULO-SD (1.40x) actually loses to ZipAR (1.88x). The supplementary Pareto analysis itself concedes that 'ZipAR dominates all other methods' on perceptual quality. The genuine advantage over the strongest baseline is confined to Tar at 1024p, so the claim of a 'new state-of-the-art' is overstated.

The practical cost profile is significant and under-quantified in the main text: the drafter has the same capacity as the target model, requiring two full sets of weights and KV-caches, plus trained up/down-samplers (MULO-SD is not training-free like its closest competitor). Memory footprint numbers are never reported.
All latency results use batch size 1 on a single A100; no throughput or batched-serving results are given, which limits generalizability of the speedup claims to realistic serving scenarios.

The comparison protocol selects MULO-SD's operating point by matching LANTERN's GenEval score, which is a defensible but selective reporting choice; no human evaluation is provided to substantiate the perceptual-quality claims, relying only on proxy metrics that move in inconsistent directions (HPSv2 drops 0.8-1.0 at 1024p while FID improves).

Reproducibility is questionable: the project-page URL in the paper is blank, no code release is stated, and results depend on ported/retrained drafters (LANTERN drafter accuracy of only 0.12 top-1 makes the EAGLE-2/LANTERN baselines potentially under-tuned, as the authors themselves acknowledge).

strengths: The core idea of combining multi-resolution drafting with upsampling inside a speculative decoding loop is a sensible and, to the authors' credit, largely unexplored direction for next-token-prediction AR image models; the paper is positioned well against LANTERN, EAGLE-2, and ZipAR.

The local rejection/expansion mechanism (Eq. 6-8) and island-wise parallel resampling are a thoughtful use of the spatial locality of visual AR models, and the ablation in Fig. 5c plus the supplementary radius study (Fig. 9) support that local expansion matters.

The evaluation is broad for this line of work: two model families (Tar-1.5B/7B, LlamaGen-XL), two target resolutions, four metrics (GenEval, DPG-Bench, FID, HPSv2), latency measured with CUDA events, and a useful supplementary latency breakdown (Fig. 7) and theoretical NFE speedup model (Eq. 10).

The limitations section is honest: it explicitly discusses the two-checkpoint memory burden, drafter-verifier distributional mismatch (which they themselves observe on LlamaGen), and points toward self-speculative decoding as a remedy.

The supplementary is substantive rather than decorative: Algorithm 1, training details for up/down-samplers, and a candid discussion of why LANTERN/EAGLE-2 underperform on Tar (low drafter Top-1 accuracy, 0.12 vs 0.38 reported in [20]).
weaknesses: The headline claim of a 'new state-of-the-art in speculative decoding for image synthesis' is contradicted by the paper's own analysis. Supplementary Fig. 8 states that 'ZipAR dominates all other methods, with mostly unchanged perceptual quality.' In Table 1, ZipAR at 1024p achieves 3.65x speedup with essentially zero metric degradation (-0.0 FID, +0.1 HPSv2 on Tar-7B), while MULO-SD's 3.90x/5.33x comes with real costs (FID -3.1, HPSv2 -0.8, and on Tar-1.5B FID 31.3 vs 32.4 is the only gain). The overclaim relative to the paper's own Pareto analysis is a material weakness, not a presentation nit.

At 512p the method does not beat the simple training-free baseline it must outperform: on LlamaGen-XL, MULO-SD is 1.40x vs ZipAR's 1.88x; on Tar-1.5B it is 1.94x vs 1.88x — a marginal gain achieved only by sweeping the acceptance threshold tau to match LANTERN's GenEval, an operating-point selection that invites cherry-picking concerns.

The cost/benefit accounting is unfavorable. ZipAR is training-free and single-checkpoint; MULO-SD requires two full model checkpoints with two KV-caches (acknowledged as potentially prohibitive), plus either trained latent up/down-samplers (~20-30M parameters each, GAN training) or a training-free but expensive pixel-space decode-decode-encode upsampling round trip. The speedup therefore buys modestly more acceleration at the price of significantly more system complexity and memory.

The relaxed acceptance rule (Eq. 5 with tau = 1e-4) makes the method an approximation with no theoretical drift control. The paper borrows LANTERN's TVD machinery (Eq. 4) in the preliminaries but the final acceptance criterion only pools probability mass against a tiny threshold, and local neighborhood resampling (Eq. 6-7) assumes accepted distant tokens are 'valid and sufficient context' — a plausible but unproven assumption with no bound or analysis of the induced distributional error. The observed FID/HPSv2 drops at aggressive tau are the empirical symptom of this.

Much of the reported speedup appears to derive from the parallel-decoding integration (ZipAR-style drafting and island resampling), i.e., existing components, rather than from multi-scale speculation per se; Fig. 5d shows parallel decoding is a large and consistent contributor, making the incremental novelty of the core multi-scale drafting harder to isolate.

Reproducibility and consistency issues: the TVD threshold delta is 0.4 in the main paper and 0.1 in the supplementary without reconciliation; the LANTERN drafter for Tar is trained on a self-chosen dataset subset ('a one-to-one comparison is not possible'), so baseline fairness relies on the authors' port; the local expansion radius l=3 for 1024p was not ablated 'due to lack of computational resource'; and no code or project page content is verifiable from the manuscript (the project-page URL is blank).

Evaluation on a single A100 with batch size 1 is a narrow deployment regime for a method whose selling point is latency; no results on newer/stronger AR backbones beyond Tar and LlamaGen-XL, and no human evaluation despite claims about perceptual quality.

strengths: Addresses a relevant and underexplored problem: accelerating next-token AR image generation (as used in unified MLLMs), where multi-scale/next-scale methods like VAR cannot be directly applied. The framing that SD for images must contend with token ambiguity and spatial structure is well motivated.

The core ideas are sensible and well integrated: (i) low-resolution drafter + up-sampler producing high-resolution drafts verified in parallel, (ii) local rejection with neighborhood expansion (Eq. 6-7) exploiting the spatial locality of visual AR models, and (iii) parallel drafting/resampling via rejection islands (Eq. 8). The local expansion rule is a genuinely useful contribution beyond raster-scan rejection.

Unusually thorough evaluation for this area: two model families (Tar-1.5B/7B, LlamaGen-XL), two target resolutions (512p/1024p), four metrics (speedup, GenEval, DPG-Bench, FID, HPSv2), multiple baselines (ZipAR, EAGLE-2, LANTERN), and extensive ablations (upsampler losses, probability pooling, local verification vs. raster-scan, expansion radius l, parallel decoding) plus a detailed latency breakdown (Fig. 7).

Strong empirical results at high resolution: up to 5.33x speedup on Tar-7B at 1024p versus 3.65x for ZipAR-16 and 1.45x for LANTERN, with near-baseline GenEval/DPG-Bench. The 1024p case is where the method is most convincing, consistent with the latency analysis showing the drafter cost becomes negligible.

Transparent reporting: the limitations section honestly discusses the two-checkpoint memory burden and drafter-verifier distributional misalignment (e.g., degraded results on LlamaGen), and the supplementary provides a full algorithm, training details, theoretical speedup model, and a drafter-quality analysis explaining why LANTERN underperforms on Tar.
weaknesses: The relaxed acceptance criterion (Eq. 5, threshold tau) abandons the exactness guarantee of speculative decoding, and unlike LANTERN's TVD-bounded relaxation, the paper provides no theoretical or empirical bound tying tau to distributional deviation from the target model. Quality is only checked post hoc via GenEval/FID/HPSv2 at selected operating points.

The headline claim of the 'best speed-quality trade-off' is undermined by the authors' own supplementary analysis (Sec. 8): 'ZipAR dominates all other methods, with mostly unchanged perceptual quality... and only slight degradation to GenEval.' At 512p on Tar-1.5B, MULO-SD (1.94x, GenEval -1.3, FID +0.4) is arguably worse than ZipAR-16 (1.88x, GenEval -1.1, FID -0.0), and ZipAR is training-free with a single model. The substantial advantage only materializes at 1024p on the 7B model (5.33x vs 3.65x).

The comparison protocol is favorable to the proposed method: tau is swept to match LANTERN's GenEval, but no quality-matched operating point is enforced against ZipAR, the strongest baseline. FID and HPSv2 trends at matched speed are not consistently favorable to MULO-SD (Fig. 8 shows FID 'tends to suffer' for MULO-SD).

Practical cost is significant: the drafter has the same capacity as the target, requiring two full sets of weights and KV-caches, and the speedup relies on resolution-specific checkpoint pairs. The method's applicability therefore depends on the increasingly common but not universal availability of multi-resolution checkpoints, and LlamaGen results confirm sensitivity to drafter-verifier alignment.

Novelty is moderate: the framework largely composes existing ingredients (LANTERN's relaxed verification, ZipAR's locality-driven parallel decoding, the multi-scale prior of VAR-style models). The genuinely new pieces (neighborhood expansion, rejection islands, the upsampling-based drafting loop) are useful but incremental. LANTERN++ [33] is cited but not compared, despite being a direct refinement of the closest baseline.

Some evaluation details weaken the measurements: the ~17s conditioning-sequence generation is excluded from latency analysis (fair for comparing decoders, but the reported end-to-end speedups are decoder-only); latency is measured at batch size 1 on a single A100; FID/HPSv2 use only 5k COCO images; and no human evaluation is provided to support the perceptual-quality claims.

Minor clarity issues: the acceptance rule in the main text (Eq. 5) differs in presentation from Algorithm 1 (which uses Ak,delta neighborhoods), and the interaction between tau, k, and delta is only loosely characterized.
